strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: inference-time mitigation of memorized training images in text-to-image diffusion models, with clear relevance to privacy and copyright risk.
The proposed GUARD formulation is simple, modular, and practically attractive: it requires no retraining and can be instantiated with different positive targets.

The paper provides a useful empirical analysis of cross-attention behavior, especially the distinction between verbatim and template memorization and the observation that fixed EOT-token attenuation is insufficient.

Evaluation covers several relevant inference-time baselines and reports memorization and quality trade-offs using SSCD, CLIP, and FID, including Pareto-style analyses and ablations over blocks, heads, timesteps, and alternative GUARD targets.

The method appears effective on the reported benchmark: CA-in-GUARD improves best SSCD substantially in SD v1.4 verbatim memorization and is competitive or better for template memorization, while generally preserving CLIP/FID reasonably well.
The limitations section appropriately acknowledges that inference-time mitigation does not remove memorized information from model weights and is not sufficient for white-box threat models.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is narrow relative to the strength of the claims. Results are limited to Stable Diffusion v1.4/v2.0 and a small filtered subset of Webster prompts: 72, 143, and 96 prompts after SSCD > 0.7 filtering. This makes claims of broad robustness across architectures and memorization types somewhat overstated.

Hyperparameter selection appears optimistic: methods are tuned separately per architecture/memorization setting and results are often selected by the target metric on the same evaluation set. Without a validation split or fixed deployment configuration, the reported gains may overestimate real-world performance.

The evaluation relies heavily on SSCD against known training images. This is reasonable for the benchmark but does not establish robustness against adaptive extraction, prompt paraphrases, seed search, stronger similarity metrics, or cases where the memorized source image is unknown.

Quality evaluation is incomplete. CLIP and FID are useful but weak proxies for prompt fidelity, image quality, and semantic preservation; no human evaluation or more targeted qualitative failure analysis is provided.

Reproducibility is weakened by a blank code link, high compute cost, incomplete details on exact grid values/seeds, and lack of confidence intervals for FID. The method also requires implementation-level intervention inside cross-attention modules, which may be nontrivial to reproduce across model families.

The method increases inference cost: CA-in-GUARD is substantially slower than no mitigation and CA attenuation, and the runtime table reports aggregate wall-clock times without enough normalization or variance to assess practical deployment cost.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports, especially phrases such as 'by far the most robust' and suggestions that universal application is safe based only on 200 non-memorized LAION prompts and only CA attenuation, not the full CA-in-GUARD method.

Originality is moderate rather than high: the work combines known ideas from classifier-free guidance arithmetic, repulsive guidance, and cross-attention attenuation. The dynamic spike detector and careful template/verbatim analysis are useful, but the conceptual leap is incremental.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: memorization mitigation in text-to-image diffusion models, with clear privacy and copyright relevance.
The proposed GUARD framing is intuitive: combine repulsion from the standard memorizing trajectory with attraction toward a modified, supposedly safer conditional prediction.

The paper includes useful empirical observations about cross-attention behavior, especially the distinction between verbatim and template memorization and the inadequacy of fixed EOT-token interventions.
The evaluation compares against several relevant inference-time baselines and includes ablations over blocks, heads, timesteps, positive targets, and non-memorized prompts.
weaknesses: The central empirical evidence is not strong enough for the paper's broad claims. The evaluation is restricted to small filtered subsets of Webster prompts, yielding only 72, 143, and 96 prompts across the main settings, so the conclusion that the method is robust across architectures and memorization types feels overstated.

The hyperparameter protocol is a serious concern. The authors tune separately per architecture, memorization type, method, and metric, then report best achievable values. This risks selecting on the evaluation set and makes the claimed dominance difficult to interpret without a held-out validation split or fixed deployment configuration.

The reported confidence intervals appear to be over four generations per prompt, but prompts are the real independent units. Treating generations as independent can substantially understate uncertainty, especially with such small prompt sets.

The method definition has technical ambiguities. The paper says it attenuates attention logits by multiplying selected logits by alpha > 0, but multiplying negative logits can make them less negative and potentially increase attention after softmax. The allowed alpha ranges also include values above 1, so it is unclear when this is attenuation versus amplification.

The evaluation metrics are insufficient to establish privacy or copyright mitigation. SSCD to known training images is useful, but the paper does not evaluate adaptive extraction, nearest-neighbor retrieval beyond the known paired image, human perceptual similarity, or whether outputs remain derivative under template memorization.

The FID protocol is questionable: FID is computed between generated images from memorized prompts and 10,000 LAION images, which is a weak proxy for generation quality and may reward distributional drift rather than prompt-specific quality preservation. No human evaluation is provided.

The strongest practical claim, that mitigation can be applied universally without knowing which prompts are memorized, is supported only by a small 200-prompt non-memorized experiment and only for CA attenuation, not for the full CA-in-GUARD method or competing methods.

The reproducibility package is incomplete in the manuscript: it states that code is available at a blank location, and several details needed to reproduce the results are underspecified, including exact prompt lists after filtering, baseline tuning grids, random seeds, model/checkpoint versions, and full implementation details for attention interception.

The originality is moderate rather than strong. The paper builds on prior work connecting memorization to cross-attention and CFG dynamics; the main novelty is a dynamic spike detector plus contrastive guidance wrapper, but the conceptual and algorithmic advance feels incremental.

The limitations section is honest about inference-time methods not removing memorized information from weights, but it does not adequately discuss adaptive adversaries, false negatives in spike detection, possible degradation on broader non-memorized prompts, or legal/ethical limits of SSCD-based mitigation.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: mitigating training-example memorization in text-to-image diffusion models at inference time, where training-time control or model finetuning may be unavailable or impractical.

The proposed GUARD framework is technically coherent and intuitive: it extends classifier-free guidance with a repulsive term away from the standard memorizing conditional trajectory and an attractive term toward a safer conditional prediction. The concrete CA-in-GUARD instantiation is well motivated by the authors' empirical analysis of cross-attention spikes.

The empirical evaluation is broader and more careful than much related work in this area. The paper separates verbatim and template memorization, filters for strongly memorized examples, evaluates SD v1.4 and SD v2.0, compares against several relevant inference-time baselines, and reports SSCD, CLIP, FID, Pareto-style tradeoffs, ablations, non-memorized prompt behavior, and runtime.

The results support the main claim that dynamic per-prompt cross-attention attenuation is more robust than fixed EOT/padding-token interventions. CA-in-GUARD is consistently strong across the three evaluated memorization settings, with especially clear gains in SSCD for SD v1.4 verbatim memorization and SD v2.0 template memorization.

The paper is generally well written and easy to follow. The distinction between the abstract GUARD framework and its cross-attention attenuation instantiation is clear, and the appendix contains useful implementation and ablation details.

The limitations and impact discussion is honest about a key threat-model boundary: inference-time mitigation does not erase memorized information from the model weights and therefore does not protect against white-box extraction.
weaknesses: The evaluation scope is still fairly narrow: all main results are on Stable Diffusion v1.4/v2.0 and a filtered subset of Webster's 500 memorized prompts, yielding only 72, 143, and 96 prompts across the three main settings. This is reasonable for a difficult memorization benchmark, but it limits confidence that the method generalizes to newer architectures, larger T2I systems, or more diverse memorization regimes.

The method is heavily tuned per architecture and memorization setting, with different hyperparameter ranges for CA attenuation and CA-in-GUARD. The paper reports ranges but not enough detail on exact grids, validation protocol, or whether tuning could overfit the small benchmark. This matters because the reported gains depend on favorable metric tradeoffs.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone. The appendix includes implementation details, hardware, GPU-hour estimates, and hyperparameter ranges, but the code link is blank, exact prompts/splits and grid values are not fully specified, and some baseline implementation details are not described enough to independently reproduce the comparisons.

The claimed efficiency advantage should be tempered. CA attenuation has small overhead, but CA-in-GUARD still increases wall-clock runtime substantially relative to no mitigation and RTA, even with batching. The text sometimes describes the method as close to a single forward pass, while the reported runtime suggests a meaningful practical cost.

The metrics are standard but imperfect. SSCD captures image-copy similarity, CLIP captures prompt alignment only coarsely, and FID against LAION references may not isolate perceptual quality for the memorized-prompt distribution. The paper would be stronger with human or stronger perceptual evaluations and qualitative failure cases.

Some claims are phrased too broadly relative to the evidence. The method is convincingly better among the tested inference-time baselines, but claims such as universal applicability to non-memorized prompts are based on only 200 LAION prompts and only CA attenuation, not the full CA-in-GUARD method or a broad deployment setting.

The paper would benefit from a deeper analysis of failure modes: when spike detection misses memorization triggers, when attenuation harms semantic fidelity, and whether adversarial prompt variants can route around the intervention. This is especially relevant because inference-time methods do not remove memorized information from the model.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: inference-time mitigation of memorization in text-to-image diffusion models, with clear relevance to privacy, copyright, and deployment risk.

The proposed GUARD formulation is simple and modular, and the concrete CA-in-GUARD instantiation is well motivated by an empirical analysis of cross-attention spikes. The distinction between verbatim and template memorization is useful and helps explain why fixed-token interventions such as EOT-only attenuation can fail.

The evaluation is broader than many papers in this area: it compares against several inference-time baselines, reports SSCD, CLIP, FID, and DINO retrieval metrics, separates memorization regimes, includes Pareto-style tradeoff analyses, provides ablations over blocks/heads/timesteps/samplers/steps/CFG scale, and includes runtime/memory measurements.

The reported gains are meaningful in several settings, especially SD v1.4 verbatim memorization and SD v2.0 template memorization. CA-in-GUARD often improves SSCD while maintaining comparable image quality, and CA attenuation alone is a useful contribution relative to prior cross-attention mitigation.
The limitations section correctly acknowledges that inference-time methods do not remove memorized information from weights and therefore do not address white-box extraction threat models.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript states that code is available, but the code URL is blank. Several implementation details needed for exact reproduction are also underspecified, including precise grids, selected hyperparameters per reported result, seed handling, prompt splits, and baseline reimplementation details.

The central safety claim is somewhat stronger than the evidence. The method is evaluated against known paired memorized training images using SSCD/DINO, but this does not establish that generations are broadly distinct from all training data or robust against adaptive prompt/search attacks.

The evaluation is largely confined to Stable Diffusion-family models and a small high-memorization subset from Webster: 72, 143, and 96 prompts in the main settings, plus only 39 SD v3.0 prompts. This makes the empirical story promising but not yet definitive for modern T2I systems or diverse memorization sources.

Hyperparameter selection is favorable to the proposed method and somewhat hard to interpret. Hyperparameters are tuned separately per architecture/memorization setting, and some figures report the best configuration per metric rather than a single deployable configuration. This is informative for Pareto analysis but weakens claims of robust default performance.

There is a technical ambiguity in the attention attenuation definition: multiplying logits by a positive alpha less than 1 attenuates positive logits but can increase negative logits toward zero before softmax. The paper should clarify whether attenuation is applied to attention probabilities, positive logits only, shifted logits, or raw logits, since this affects the method's interpretation and reproducibility.

The method assumes that mitigation can be applied at generation time, but the paper does not fully study deployment questions such as how to detect when to apply it, performance on broad user prompts, false positives beyond a small 200-prompt non-memorized test, or adaptive users who vary prompts to recover memorized content.

Presentation is generally clear, but the paper is somewhat overclaimed in places: phrases such as “by far the most robust” and “guarding against reproducing training data” exceed what is demonstrated by the finite benchmark and non-adaptive evaluation.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: inference-time mitigation of memorization in text-to-image diffusion models, with clear practical motivation for settings where retraining or unlearning is infeasible.

The proposed GUARD framing is intuitive and modular: combining repulsion from the standard prompt-conditioned trajectory with attraction toward a modified, lower-memorization conditioning signal is a reasonable idea.

The empirical study covers several relevant baselines and multiple Stable Diffusion versions, separates verbatim and template memorization, and includes useful ablations over blocks, heads, timesteps, samplers, CFG scales, and metrics such as SSCD, CLIP, FID, and DINO.

The paper identifies a plausible limitation of prior EOT-only attention attenuation methods: template memorization does not appear to be explained by EOT attention alone, motivating per-prompt spike detection.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The main evaluation is on small filtered subsets: 72 prompts for SD v1.4 verbatim, 143 for SD v1.4 template, and 96 for SD v2.0 template. The SD v3.0 result uses only 39 prompts with SSCD > 0.3. This is too narrow to justify broad claims such as being 'by far the most robust' mitigation method across architectures and memorization types.

The evaluation protocol risks optimistic model selection. Hyperparameters are tuned separately for each architecture-memorization setting and results often report the best configuration for each target metric, apparently using the evaluation prompts themselves rather than a held-out validation split. This makes comparisons less convincing, especially with small sample sizes.

Reproducibility is weak. The appendix says 'Code. The code for reproducing the results is available at:' but provides no URL. Important implementation details for baselines, exact grids, seeds, prompt lists after filtering, and generated outputs are not sufficiently specified for reliable reproduction.

The method description has technical ambiguities. The paper says logits for detected tokens are multiplied by alpha > 0 to attenuate attention, but multiplying negative logits by alpha < 1 can increase their softmax probability. The reported tau ranges also conflict with the text's example of tau = 3, with verbatim settings using very small thresholds such as 0.01-0.3, which calls into question how selective the spike detector really is.

Several quality metrics are not fully reliable in the reported setup. FID is computed on very small generated sample sets for the filtered benchmark and has no confidence intervals. CLIP scores for template settings are very low, and many mitigation gains come with noticeable prompt-alignment degradation, yet the discussion often frames quality preservation too strongly.

The paper does not adequately address deployment assumptions. It mostly evaluates prompts already known to be memorized or filtered by SSCD against training images. The practical problem of detecting when to apply mitigation without access to the original training image, and the behavior under adaptive or adversarial prompting, remains underdeveloped.

The limitations and ethics discussion is incomplete. The paper notes that inference-time methods do not remove memorized information from weights, but it gives little treatment of privacy/copyright risks, misuse, residual leakage under repeated sampling, or responsible release of memorized prompt/image examples.

Presentation is generally readable, but the paper is rhetorically inflated and occasionally imprecise. Claims such as 'surgical,' 'safe target,' and 'by far' are stronger than what the experiments establish, and some tables/figures rely on selection protocols that are hard to interpret at a glance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: inference-time mitigation of memorization in text-to-image diffusion models, with clear practical relevance for privacy and copyright risk.

The core idea is technically sensible: GUARD combines repulsion from the standard memorizing conditional trajectory with attraction toward a modified, prompt-aligned positive target. The concrete cross-attention spike attenuation mechanism is well motivated by the authors' empirical analysis of token-level attention patterns.

The evaluation is stronger than typical for this area. It covers SD v1.4 and SD v2.0, verbatim and template memorization, several recent inference-time baselines, SSCD/CLIP/FID metrics, DINO-based retrieval metrics, qualitative examples, and many ablations over blocks, heads, timesteps, samplers, step counts, CFG scales, and alternative GUARD targets.

The results are convincing overall: CA-in-GUARD generally improves memorization reduction while preserving competitive image quality, and it is especially compelling that the method remains robust across template memorization settings where fixed EOT-based attention methods perform poorly.

The limitations discussion is honest about the central threat-model boundary: inference-time mitigation does not remove memorized information from model weights and cannot protect against white-box extraction. This is appropriately framed rather than hidden.
The method appears computationally practical. CA attenuation has near-baseline overhead, and CA-in-GUARD has moderate overhead while remaining lighter than several baselines in memory usage.
weaknesses: The reproducibility package is incomplete as written: the appendix says 'Code. The code for reproducing the results is available at:' but provides no URL or artifact. Given the method relies on careful attention interception, batching, and hyperparameter choices, this is a material reproducibility weakness that should be fixed before publication.

The hyperparameter selection protocol may be optimistic. Hyperparameters are tuned separately per architecture, memorization type, method, and target metric, apparently on the same benchmark used for reporting. This makes the reported best-achievable and trade-off results informative but less predictive of out-of-distribution performance without a validation/test split or a fixed deployment recipe.

The main evaluation uses relatively small high-memorization subsets after filtering, e.g. 72, 143, and 96 prompts. The authors do include a full-spectrum evaluation, which helps, but the strongest claims still rest on a benchmark of known memorized prompts and may not fully capture real deployment conditions where memorized prompts are unknown or distributionally different.

The SD v3.0 evaluation is useful but weakly powered and not fully comparable: only 39 prompts pass the relaxed SSCD threshold, several baselines are inapplicable, and the architecture differs substantially from the U-Net setting that motivates much of the analysis.

The safety framing is somewhat narrow. The method reduces memorized generations under standard sampling but does not evaluate adaptive adversaries who can vary prompts, seeds, CFG, or repeated queries to bypass inference-time mitigation, despite acknowledging white-box limitations.

Some quality metrics are limited. CLIP and FID can miss prompt fidelity and perceptual degradation, and FID is computed on small generated sets in the filtered evaluations without confidence intervals. Human evaluation or stronger image-quality/prompt-alignment measures would make the quality-preservation claim more robust.
